contents.text: The stability of an isotope's nucleus depends on whether the repulsive electrostatic forces between protons and the attractive nuclear forces between nucleons are balanced. These forces are balanced and the isotope is stable when the isotope's neutron-to-proton ratio is favorable. When this ratio is unfavorable, the forces in the nucleus are unbalanced and the isotope is radioactive.

For elements with 20 or fewer protons, the favorable neutron-to-proton ratio is about one to one. The favorable ratio increases as the number of protons increases because it takes an even greater number of neutrons to counter the electrostatic repulsions across a larger nucleus.

This graph shows the number of neutrons and protons in each known isotope. The green line shows a neutron-to-proton ratio of one to one, the orange dots represent unstable isotopes, and the blue dots represent stable isotopes. The heaviest stable isotope, lead-208, is labeled.

contents.text: The stability of an isotope's nucleus depends on whether the repulsive electrostatic forces between protons and the attractive nuclear forces between nucleons are balanced. These forces are balanced and the isotope is stable when the isotope's neutron-to-proton ratio is favorable. When this ratio is unfavorable, the forces in the nucleus are unbalanced and the isotope is radioactive.

For elements with 20 or fewer protons, the favorable neutron-to-proton ratio is about one to one. The favorable ratio increases as the number of protons increases because it takes an even greater number of neutrons to counter the electrostatic repulsions across a larger nucleus.

This graph shows the number of neutrons and protons in each known isotope. The green line shows a neutron-to-proton ratio of one to one, the orange dots represent unstable isotopes, and the blue dots represent stable isotopes. The heaviest stable isotope, lead-208, is labeled.
